articles.headline: 2026's Bloodiest Game Just Got a Release Date
keyFacts: Developer Eksil Team announced that the martial arts beat-'em-up game Acts of Blood will be released for Windows PC on Dec. 4.
The game will also launch on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X consoles sometime in 2027.
Players control a character named Hendra on a quest for revenge through Indonesia, featuring brutal combat inspired by films like The Raid.
body: While big gaming showcases like The Game Awards are packed full of big-budget games, they usually feature plenty of exciting indies, too. Acts of Blood was spotlighted at last year's Summer Game Fest, and it immediately piqued our interest. It's a martial arts beat-'em-up inspired by movies like The Raid. Think Sifu, but with even more blood.

On Wednesday, developer Eksil Team announced that Acts of Blood will be released for Windows PC on Dec. 4. It was previously only officially announced for PC, but Eksil Team has good news for console gamers too: Acts of Blood will land on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X sometime in 2027.

If you don't want to wait, you can get a taste of Acts of Blood's combat in its demo on Steam. That demo has over 1,500 Very Positive player reviews, with players enjoying its brutal combat. "Great animations, weighty feeling combat, and simple but meaningful feeling combos," one player wrote in their review. "The Raid is a freaking AWESOME movie and now you can play it," another said.
Acts of Blood plot and gameplay details

Acts of Blood is like The Raid meets John Wick. You'll play as Hendra as he seeks out revenge, ostensibly by beating up hundreds of dudes throughout various hallways and other locales. Here's its official description:

When justice fails, Hendra embarks on a personal quest for revenge that will take him through the bustling streets of Bandapa, Indonesia to uncover the powerful group behind his family’s murder and make them pay for their actions.
Learn, develop and improve Hendra’s combat skills, unlock punishing new moves, and become a martial arts master to beat down waves of enemies, defeat powerful bosses, and avenge your family.

It started as a solo project from developer Fajrul FN, but his friends gradually joined over time, leading to Fajrul FN taking charge of the small indie team Eksil Team. Last summer, I chatted with Fajrul FN about developing Acts of Blood and its inspirations. "For gameplay, it’s a blend of Sleeping Dogs’ counter-based combat and Sifu’s layered combo mechanics. We’re also taking visual cues from games like Max Payne and Manhunt, especially when it comes to grit and tone," he said.

Martial arts is at the core of Acts of Blood's gameplay, with a variety of strikes, counters, and finishers available. There will be an improvisational element too, as you can attack with melee weapons, pick up firearms, and use the environment against foes. "We’re going all-in on violence as a core part of the experience. Brutal takedowns, dismemberment, and yes, our own version of X-ray kills," Fajrul FN said. "We’ve been clear with our partners from the start: this isn’t going to hold back."
To any of us who have enjoyed the brutality of action movies like The Furious or fighting games like Mortal Kombat, that's music to our ears. Acts of Blood will start throwing hands on PC on Dec. 4.

articles.headline: Urine Trouble: PEE V PEE, a multiplayer game about hiding from the cops while you take a whizz on public property, takes the trophy for punniest title of the year
keyFacts: Urine Trouble: PEE V PEE is a competitive online multiplayer game where players urinate on public property to score points.
Rebel players called The Pissers try to avoid detection by blending in with identical NPCs while real players act as cops to hunt them down.
Players can currently sign up for a playtest or wishlist the game on Steam.
body: I've been doing this whole games journalism for over five years now, and I've seen a lot of different kinds of games in that time. I've written about plenty of them too, with a fair few being plenty weird. But I'll admit that today's game is one that I do understand if I were to tell anyone I'm interested in playing who maybe isn't familiar with games as a whole, they'd probably talk to someone else at the party. You see, Urine Trouble: PEE V PEE is a competitive online game all about pissing literally everywhere, and trying not to get caught doing so.

In Urine Trouble: PEE V PEE, public urination has become punishable by death. "Good!" I hear those of you who hate when people randomly piss on the side of a building, though perhaps the death penalty is an overreaction. As a response to this, a group of rebels known as The Pissers decide to take back their city by pissing on literally everything. Luckily, you, as a Pisser, are able to blend in with the NPCs of the world in order to hide from the cops, as every single character looks almost exactly the same.
Watch on YouTube

Your goal then is to rack up as many points as you can by whizzing all over public property, all while trying to act like an NPC while the cops aren't around. Oh, and those cops are also played by real people, who will in fact kill you if they figure out that you're one of The Pissers. They appear to have limited amounts of ammo, so have to be careful how they're used, and guessing wrong means flat out killing civilians. The whole thing is obviously quite ridiculous, but that double pun title just really shows how much more work the rest of the games industry needs to do to come up with good names for their games.

I can't actually tell you much more than that because, well, Valve won't let me look at the Steam page due to the UK's whole Online Safety Act nonsense, and like hell I'm getting a credit card just for the pissing game. articles.headline: Dying in ICE custody: Inside one family’s story of heartbreak
keyFacts: Ismael Ayala-Uribe died in ICE custody at the Adelanto facility on September 22, 2025, from complications of a pelvic abscess.
Experts, watchdogs, and an internal review stated that inadequate medical treatment and delayed emergency care caused his preventable death.
Human Rights Watch reported that immigrants in ICE custody are dying at a rate roughly three times higher under Trump than under Biden.
body: Los Angeles, California – Saturdays marked a weekly pilgrimage for Lucia Uribe. Every weekend, she would travel to the edge of California's desert to visit her son, Ismael Ayala-Uribe, in detention.
Ismael was among the hundreds of thousands of people swept up in United States President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.

Born in Mexico and brought to the US as a child, he was arrested on August 17 while working at a car wash. Ever since, he had been in the custody of immigration authorities, first at a local jail and later at a detention centre for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Adelanto, California.
But one Saturday was different. Lucia remembers that Ismael’s hands looked paler, his eyes were bloodshot, and the fever he had was rising.
“Mom, I’m not going to make it,” Lucia recalls Ismael telling her. There was little she could do but reassure him.
“I told him, ‘Oh, my son, just hang in there as long as you can,’” Lucia said. “When I said goodbye to him, I felt something in my chest, a tightness, and it made me want to cry.”
It was the last time she would see her son alive. Lucia’s fears were confirmed by a knock at her door two days later, when police told her that her son had died at 2:32am on September 22, 2025.
Ismael was one of more than 50 people to die in ICE custody during the first 500 days of Trump's second term.
A coroner's report from the San Bernardino County Sheriff's Department in southern California found that his death was caused by complications from an abscess in his pelvic region.
Ismael's family, however, has argued that insufficient medical treatment in ICE facilities led a preventable infection to fester into a deadly condition.

For months, the Al Jazeera documentary series Fault Lines has spoken to people in ICE custody and the families of those who never made it out alive, to understand the conditions that could have led to deaths like Ismael's.
What it found was that 2025, the year Ismael died, was the deadliest year in history for those in ICE custody. But experts fear 2026 is on track to match or surpass that record.
'Not proportional'
The Trump administration has consistently denied reports that deaths in ICE custody are increasing.
In a social media post in June, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, claimed that the death rate has remained "consistent with data over the last decade".
"There has been NO spike in deaths," the department wrote, pointing to the percentage of deaths relative to the overall population of ICE detainees.
But experts and watchdog organisations warn that ICE's framing may be misleading.
“What has often been claimed is that the overall detained population is going up," said Nicholas Cuneo, an expert in immigrant health with Physicians for Human Rights, an advocacy organisation.
But he pointed to statistics that show the death rate has nearly tripled. “That clearly is not proportional to the detained population," Cuneo said.

In June, Human Rights Watch published a report revealing that, since Trump returned to office, immigrants in ICE custody are dying at a rate roughly three times higher than under his predecessor Joe Biden.

The annualised mortality rate during Biden's four-year term was 2.24 for every 10,000 detainees. Since Trump began his second term, that proportion has risen to 6.38 deaths for every 10,000 people in custody.
In total, 33 people died in ICE custody last year, according to the agency's own statistics. So far in 2026, at least 26 people have died.
Reagan Williams, a human rights lawyer and researcher who worked on the June report, said that the increase in overall detentions does not explain the spike in deaths.
"The administration has incarcerated record numbers of immigrants," Williams said.
"And yet this rapid rise in detention does not fully account for the staggering increase in deaths. A higher percentage of detained immigrants are dying under this administration."

While overcrowding at ICE facilities is a factor, experts at Physicians for Human Rights also found a pattern of delayed emergency care, understaffing and failure to provide adequate medical treatment.
Those factors have raised concerns that many ICE deaths may have been preventable, including Ismael’s.
'A major failure'
A round-faced man with dark-rimmed glasses, a moustache and short-trimmed hair, Ismael came to the US when he was only five years old.
Southern California became his home, and as an adult, he qualified for the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) programme, which offered temporary protection against deportation.
He lost his DACA status, however, in 2015 after a conviction for driving under the influence.
His family remembers him as a caring son and uncle, always willing to buy his niece and nephew new clothes or school supplies.
“Ismael was always looking after his siblings. He just had a big heart,” said his brother, Jose Miguel Ayala. “He was very protective of not just us, but my mum and dad too.”
He was 39 years old when he was brought to the Adelanto ICE Processing Center.
Two weeks after his arrival, Ismael told his family that he developed a high fever and a painful sore on his backside.

On September 18, 2025, workers at Adelanto initiated a Code Blue alert for Ismael, signalling a life-threatening medical emergency. Medical staff rushed him from his dorm to the infirmary in a wheelchair.
ICE documents show that Ismael was given pain medication, an ointment and a fibre supplement.
But according to Physicians for Human Rights' Cuneo, who reviewed the case, Ismael should have received a physical examination and antibiotics.
"That is a major failure," Cuneo said.
That weekend, hours after Lucia’s visit, Ismael’s condition worsened. Just after midnight on Sunday, ICE records say he was vomiting, shaking and sweating.
According to ICE documents, he was later sent to an intensive care unit, where he went into cardiac arrest within minutes of his arrival and subsequently died.
“I believe Ismael’s death could have fully been prevented by timely care,” Cuneo said. “It was a simple abscess that was not treated in a timely manner.”
Fault Lines obtained a coroner's investigation that reveals Ismael was critically ill when he first arrived at the hospital, a fact that was left out of ICE's public report on his death.

The coroner's report also contradicts ICE's timeline for Ismael's death. It indicates Ismael went into cardiac arrest early on September 21, nearly a full day before he passed away. Medical staff, however, managed to restore his heartbeat after intubating him.

That conflicts with ICE's report, which only notes his pulse stopping once: shortly before his death was announced on the morning of September 22. ICE described his condition on September 21 as "calm and cooperative", but it signalled no heart problems.
“If they had given him the medical care and what he needed, maybe he would be here with us,” Lucia said.
In a statement about Ismael’s death, ICE said detainees receive “comprehensive medical care” throughout their time in custody.
But California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta told Fault Lines that his office found “the exact opposite" during its inspections of the state's detention centres.
“We've gone to these facilities. We've gone into Adelanto. We have done our own physical inspections," Bonta explained.
“If what the ICE spokesperson said was true, Mr Ayala-Uribe would be with us today.”

An internal mortality review committee also found that the care provided to Ismael at Adelanto "deviated beyond safe limits of practice", according to a document obtained by US media earlier this year.
It also suggests that medical staff delayed responding to calls about Ismael's declining health in the days leading up to his death.
'We want to go outside alive, not dead'
Fault Lines spoke to current detainees in the Adelanto detention centre who say they, too, fear the conditions could be harmful to their health.
Many described inadequate medical care, mouldy food and retaliation for protesting against the subpar conditions.
Some are part of a class-action lawsuit, filed in January, accusing the US government of "inhumane and illegal conditions" at Adelanto.
"They don't take things seriously," one detainee, Kurt Campbell, said of the Adelanto staff.

"They think everyone's a liar. So when you're going through something and you express what you're going through, they act like you're lying. We do want to go outside, but we want to go outside alive, not dead."
Four men have died in Adelanto between September 2025 and March 2026, including Ismael. Campbell, who is originally from Jamaica, said he knew one of the detainees who passed away.
"His last days were spent in confinement and in Adelanto instead of being with his family," Campbell said. "He didn't kill anyone. He didn't hurt anyone. His crime was coming over the border."
Guadalupe Moreno Cristin, another detainee in Adelanto, recalls experiencing rectal bleeding for more than a week, in addition to heart issues.
When he was taken to the infirmary, the only treatment he said he was given was Tylenol and a serum. His health has continued to deteriorate.
"I haven't had a bath for, like, eight days now because I can't lift my hands up," Cristin said. "I can't change myself on my own. I can't stand for long, and I can't walk much."

Detainee Jesus Jacobo Ortiz Ruiz estimated that, for every 320 people in ICE custody, there is only one doctor. "You've got to be literally dying in here for you to get sent to the hospital," Ruiz added.
Fault Lines spoke to US Representative Judy Chu, who represents a congressional district near Adelanto. For the past decade, she has been conducting oversight visits at the facility.
"I've seen firsthand for over a decade how they've cut corners, how they don't want to spend money on food, and most importantly, they don't want to spend money on medical care," Chu said.
To push for change, roughly 150 detainees signed a petition and went on hunger strike earlier this year to denounce the "unbearable and inhuman" conditions at Adelanto.
Campbell said he was placed into solitary confinement for 30 days for participating in the hunger strike. Other detainees reported receiving physical retaliation, including Ashraf Abujama.
"They just enjoy using force on me," Abujama said. "They want to just use me as an example to all the detainees, that '[this is] what we can do'."
'An emptiness that wasn't there before'
In recent weeks, changes have been under way at Adelanto.
The facility, formerly owned by the private prison firm Geo Group, has been sold to the Department of Homeland Security for $950m, as the federal government seeks to acquire more detention centres.
Critics, however, warn that the switch to federal ownership could make conditions inside Adelanto more opaque, limiting the ability of state and local authorities to exercise their oversight roles.
It is a change that concerns families of detainees like Ismael. Where once his mother Lucia visited him at Adelanto, she now spends her weekends with a new ritual: visiting his grave on Sundays.
Jose, Ismael’s brother, often joins her, along with his sister and her two kids.
Their father often stays behind. "My dad still has a hard time going," Jose explained.
More than a year has passed, but the entire family is still grappling with the loss.
"There's a time where I just feel like he's just going to walk in," Jose said. "There's just an emptiness that wasn't there before."

articles.headline: Why even a Democratic wave might not stop Trump
keyFacts: Polling shows Democrats leading generic midterm ballots as President Donald Trump's approval ratings fall to second-term lows, Vox reported.
The author reported that Trump has expanded executive power and secured court rulings to advance his agenda without congressional support.
The article notes that if Democrats take Congress, they could launch investigations, pursue impeachment, and block Trump's judicial nominees.
body: President Donald Trump speaks on stage at the Butler-Vandalia Student Activity Center during a campaign rally on October 3, 2026, in Vandalia, Ohio. | Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images

Welcome to The Midterms, Actually. Every week I’ll be writing about two things: one big idea or trend I see forming across the 2026 primaries, and one thing I’m hearing from a voice on the ground. Let’s get into it.
One big idea: How much can Democrats slow down Trump?
A tricky thing to communicate about the upcoming midterms is that, at the federal level, the impact may not be what’s expected, at least when it comes to slowing President Donald Trump’s agenda.

Hear me out. Say the blue wave predicted by most polling materializes on November 3, and Democrats take the House and even squeak out a slim Senate majority. What happens next? Does that stop Trump from executing his agenda? Does the White House moderate its message in response to an electoral backlash?
The evidence suggests no.
Because the backlash is real, the political incentives aren’t.

Let me explain: The numbers do look rough for Trump. Pew had his approval rating at 30 percent in a survey conducted September 28 to October 4, the lowest of his second term, with Democrats up eight on the generic House ballot. Reuters/Ipsos had him at 32 percent in early October. Polling averages are a bit higher, roughly 37 percent to 39 percent depending on the aggregator. Ballotpedia’s September average put Democrats at 50 percent on the generic ballot to Republicans’ 43 percent.

But none of that is moving him. Trump is fundamentally shameless, untethered to traditional political incentives, and increasingly unhinged in his second term. He initiated a war with Iran that quite literally no one wanted. He’s plowing ahead with renewed mass deportation efforts even as Republicans urge him to abort the mission. He’s more unpopular by the month, and more consumed by vanity projects in Washington: the White House ballroom, a federal takeover of a DC golf course, whatever’s happening at the reflecting pool.

More importantly, he’s been quietly preparing for this moment of backlash, legally and politically. If there’s one theme of Trump’s second term, beyond the promises of retribution, it’s his drive to grow executive power to the point where he’s insulated from political consequences. And the courts have largely backed him.
Let ’ s run the tape

The legacy of Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency was less about finding waste, fraud, and abuse than about asserting presidential power over the federal bureaucracy. Trump has brought independent agencies to heel, firing members of the National Labor Relations Board and the Federal Trade Commission. In Trump v. Slaughter , the Supreme Court sided with him 6-3, overturning the 90-year-old Humphrey’s Executor precedent that had limited when presidents could remove agency heads. (The one notable exception: The Court refused, 5-4, to let him remove Fed governor Lisa Cook for now.)

His immigration push included federalizing National Guard troops for domestic purposes. He’s pursued unilateral military action that breaks precedent, like the Caribbean boat strikes on suspected drug smugglers. And he’s picked another fight with Congress that’s headed to court, unilaterally withholding roughly $800 million in congressionally approved funds from 11 programs supporting refugees and asylum-seekers, minority business development, housing counseling, and more.

To be clear, I don’t believe this anti-democratic throughline is happenstance. Trump has systematically used his first two years back in office to grow the power of the presidency and find ways to execute his agenda without Congress, as he did with his many tariffs — which he also claims, wrongly, that he can use to personally authorize $5,000 checks . His MAGA base has always believed the ends justify the means, but this White House has gone a step further, making clear it won’t be constrained by pesky things like federal law, separation of powers, and checks and balances. More explicitly, it openly subscribes to the “unitary executive” theory advanced in Project 2025, which argues, in essence, that the president has total control over the executive branch, including agencies like the FBI and Justice Department that have traditionally exercised some independence.

Don’t believe me? Here’s Trump at a Turning Point conference in 2019: “Then I have an Article II, where I have the right to do whatever I want as president.” Or early in his second term: “ He who saves his Country does not violate any Law .”

Stephen Miller said the quiet part out loud last year, too. In an interview on CNN’s News Central , he froze after asserting that the president has “ plenary authority ,” meaning Trump’s power is unreviewable and unquestioned.

And here’s a line from Project 2025, which basically foretold our current constitutional crisis: The next Republican White House “must take seriously the duty to protect the powers and privileges of the President from encroachments by Congress, the judiciary, and the administrative components of departments and agencies.”
Is that how democracy works?
So what does that mean for the midterms?
Of course, it’s tricky to be predictive. But when I hear Democrats say a new congressional majority will hold Trump accountable, I wonder if they should qualify those promises with a reality check.

No blue wave can overcome the structural realities of gerrymandering, which has collapsed the number of competitive districts and disincentivized compromise. Cook Political Report found that mid-decade redistricting cut the number of competitive House seats from 87 to 77, meaning Democrats now need to win 57 of those 77 to take the chamber, up from 59 of 87 under the old lines. Cook projected Republicans gaining roughly eight seats from the redraws, Democrats two. Cook’s David Wasserman has noted that fewer than 5 percent of Americans are living in the districts that will truly decide House control. Control of the House is still up for grabs, but the narrower playing field makes sweeping change much harder.

No wave can overcome conservative control of the courts, which has only grown in Trump’s second term. And most crucially, a wave matters less to a White House that thinks in such absolute terms, and sees Congress as something to be overcome, not worked with.

In a typical administration, all the conditions for Trump’s last two years would point toward de-escalation. The public has fallen out of love with the administration’s priorities, he won’t be on the ballot in 2028, and Republicans would theoretically be freer to chart their own course.

But as Trump has proven time and again, there’s no guarantee those rules apply to him, or to this version of the GOP. If anything, the 2024 presidential primary showed that Republicans are more likely to rally around Trump when they feel he’s being targeted by liberal Democrats.
That doesn’t mean the midterms don’t matter

Far from it. As we explored on America, Actually last week, there are important state and local races that will determine Americans’ access to healthcare, abortion rights, and more. The results will shape how each party approaches 2028. And a Democratic-led House or Senate could certainly make Trump’s life harder, particularly through investigations or impeachment efforts or by blocking cabinet picks and judicial nominees.
Trump will go down fighting to make Project 2025 our reality, and no matter what happens in November, the first two years were just the start.
But the question I get most often on the road is: Will November stop Trump’s agenda? To that, I think it’s important to be skeptical.

Politically, Trump is unlikely to exit stage left gracefully, and will likely hog the spotlight even as the GOP kicks off its primary to replace him. More importantly, he’s spent two years showing his hand, prioritizing an all-powerful executive branch that can thumb its nose at anyone who interferes.

The lame-duck stretch of a presidency is typically its sleepiest, as the administration focuses on limiting damage to its legacy and setting up a smooth succession. With Trump, I expect the opposite. He’ll go down fighting to make Project 2025 our reality, and no matter what happens in November, the first two years were just the start.
One thing I’m hearing

This week, we talked to Estefanía Pinto Ruiz , a democracy‚ immigration, and rural communities reporter for Enlace Latino NC. Considering how central Latino voters are to this year’s midterm elections, I wanted to ask her about her coverage of that community in North Carolina, an important battleground state.
You reported on Latino voters’ exposure to political misinformation in Spanish. What did you learn about how language and platforms shape the information voters encounter?
One key lesson I learned from my reporting is that language and other media-related factors affect access to and understanding of political information․

A survey conducted by Marisa Abrajano‚ a political science professor at the University of California San Diego‚ found that Latinos who got news from Spanish-language social media were 11 percentage points more likely to believe political falsehoods in the survey than Latinos who got news from English-language social media․

But a major distinction is that the research found a correlation but not a causal link between the two behaviors․ Reading news in Spanish doesn’t mean people are more likely to be exposed to misinformation․

Another important takeaway is the role of social media and video sites like WhatsApp and YouTube․ Many Latino adults rely on these sites along with or in place of Spanish-language media sources for political news․ News they receive on WhatsApp from family and friends can shape their views of information from other sources․
Your newsroom has asked readers to share election information they’re unsure about. What questions or claims are coming in, and what do they reveal about the confusion voters are facing?

Oftentimes people are unsure about the basic mechanism of voting: where they are supposed to vote, what their ballot will look like, or what happens if they encounter an issue at the polls. The confusion can also often come from information shared by official sources. For example, we’ve covered voters who received letters from the State Board of Elections asking them to review their registration information and worried about what that meant for their right to vote. We’ve also reported on allegations of misinformation during voter registration drives, including cases in which canvassers were falsely presented as election officials.
Beyond those stories, what are you hearing locally about the midterms that you think the national political conversation is missing?

First, the top issue is the cost of living: groceries, rent, utilities, and gas. Immigration enforcement comes close behind, but voters hold both worries at once, and they don’t vote as a monolithic bloc. Conservative and progressive groups here both say voters judge candidates on tangible outcomes, not party loyalty.

Second, this electorate is young, and that youth is often mistaken for apathy. Roughly a third of eligible Latino voters in North Carolina are under 25, and the median age is 35, compared with 48 for the state’s electorate overall. In my reporting at Enlace Latino NC, I see many first-generation citizens whose parents stayed away from US politics because of experiences with corruption or violence in their home countries. Emanuel Ramirez, 20, an NC State student, said his father fled a military coup in Guatemala and his mother violence in Colombia, and that his parents avoided US politics because they knew how dangerous political involvement could be. Emanuel taught himself the process and pre-registered at 16. Grassroots groups are using peer-to-peer outreach, often in Spanglish, to make voting less intimidating for families navigating it for the first time.

Third, national attention tends to center on federal policy, but state and local decisions are directly shaping how this election is run. Voters and advocates tell us that changing rules can create real hurdles, especially for first-time voters. Wake County replaced the long-standing Talley Student Union polling site at NC State with the Business Services Center as part of a record 18 early voting sites. While officials say they have expanded access countywide, students note that far more people voted early at Talley in 2020 and 2024 than at the replacement site.

Meanwhile, state election guidelines for processing mail-in ballots have tightened: Mail-in ballots will not be counted if the inner envelope is unsealed or signatures do not match, among other changes. Additionally, the State Board of Elections is sending letters asking 1,599 registered voters, flagged as potential noncitizens by a federal database, to confirm their citizenship or face removal from the rolls. While officials clarify that letter recipients can still vote, critics note the database is prone to errors, and advocates worry the notices could discourage eligible citizens right before early voting.

articles.headline: Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro pleads not guilty to torture charges
keyFacts: Former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores pleaded not guilty on Thursday to newly unsealed US torture charges.
The couple is accused of leading a state-sponsored repression campaign that tortured prisoners during Maduro's presidency from 2013 to 2026.
Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein scheduled their trial to begin on June 14, 2027, following their seizure by the US military.
body: Former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro appeared in court on Thursday, where he rejected newly unsealed torture charges against him and his wife, Cilia Flores.
He said the indictment represented "false accusations" against him.
Maduro was combative in court as he was asked to enter a plea to the charges, condemning allegations of torture as "false accusations and false testimony."
Ultimately, Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein interjected to declare that "a plea of not guilty will be entered on behalf of Mr. Maduro."
Flores told the judge through the Spanish interpreter: "I am completely innocent. I am not guilty."

The court appearance was the latest for the pair, who are currently in US custody in New York City, now eight months since they were seized from their Caracas home by the US military in a nighttime raid.
The new torture charges against the couple have been added to the drug-trafficking charges they previously faced.
Maduro and Flores' trial is set to begin June 14, 2027, according to a schedule approved by the judge Thursday.
What are the torture charges?
Maduro and his wife have been accused of leading a state-sponsored repression campaign that tortured scores of victims, including three Americans, during his presidency from 2013 to 2026.
They are said to have committed human rights violations as part of a scheme to hold on to power.
Security forces have been accused of torturing prisoners with electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro's behest.
Maduro stands accused of personally recommending torture methods, receiving updates on specific victims' treatment, and threatening to kill one prisoner's child as a form of psychological torture.
For her part, Cilia Flores has been accused of helping develop the repressive system and ordering the torture of some specific people, the indictment alleges.
Human rights groups have long accused Venezuelan officials of torturing detainees, but the US indictment marks the first time that Maduro could be held to account over the allegations.

Maudro has been under investigation by the International Criminal Court (ICC) over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents, but the court has not served him with a warrant.
Torture is considered a crime under international law and can be prosecuted outside of the nation where the abuse occurred and regardless of the victims' nationality.

But in the US, the prosecution of foreign officials is exceedingly rare. The only recent cases include the son of Liberian President Charles Taylor, Russians responsible for war crimes in Ukraine and a former prison warden in Bashar Assad's Syria.
Edited by: Wesley Dockery

articles.headline: US justice department sues California over alleged noncitizen voting
keyFacts: The US Department of Justice sued California to prevent the state from tabulating certain mail-in ballots in the midterm elections.
California election officials refused to process a federal list of 20,000 flagged voters, citing security and voter-purge concerns.
The lawsuit asks a federal court to require California to set aside and verify flagged ballots before counting them.
body: The US Department of Justice sued California on Thursday, seeking a court order to prevent the state from tabulating certain ballots cast in the midterm elections.

The suit came two days after the department made a specious demand to the state. On Tuesday, the department sent election officials in Los Angeles county a thumb drive with a handwritten password purporting to contain the names of noncitizens registered to vote. The department asked officials to confirm the citizenship of anyone on the list and set aside ballots from those whose status could not be confirmed. It gave the state 48 hours – an extremely narrow window – to take action. It did not provide details on how it came up with the names on the list. In its lawsuit, filed in federal court in the central district of California, the justice department said it had provided the state with more than 20,000 names of likely noncitizens.
The Los Angeles county clerk and recorder, Dean Logan, said his office would not review the list, in part because it didn’t consider the USB drive secure.

In a statement on Wednesday, the California secretary of state, Shirley Weber, a Democrat, said the justice department had not provided the list of voters to her office. “The [justice department’s] relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states’ protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections,” Weber said.
Justice department lawyers are asking the court to order the state not to count votes from those it had flagged.

“This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote-by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter’s citizenship status can be determined,” the lawsuit said. “This Court should order California (1) to set aside vote-by-mail ballots from persons identified by the Federal Government likely to be noncitizens and (2) to independently – or in collaboration with the Federal Government – verify their citizenship status (beyond relying on unverified statements of citizenship necessary to registering) before tabulating their vote-by-mail ballot.”

The request to block tabulation comes amid concerns that Donald Trump and his allies will interfere in the counting of votes in the midterm elections, in which Republicans are expected to lose seats in Congress.

The Trump administration’s methodology for identifying noncitizens has come under scrutiny. Earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said there could be as many as 278,000 noncitizens on the rolls in four states, including more than 190,000 in California and about 16,000 in Nevada.

Officials at the DHS refused to share their methodology with Nevada election officials and later turned over just 185 names of people it had a strong belief were noncitizens. When Nevada officials investigated, they found every one of those people was a citizen.

Richard Hasen, an election law scholar at UCLA, described the justice department’s efforts in California as “a nice publicity stunt that gets attention for [the justice department] and reinforces the notion among the president’s most ardent supporters that California is not doing enough to combat voter fraud”.

“The Department of Justice has no standing to tell states and localities to go in and remove voters from voting rolls in the midst of an election. In fact, the National Voter Registration Act bars systematic purges of ineligible voters in the 90-day period before the election,” he wrote in a blogpost. “The purpose of this provision, unsurprisingly, is to stop false positives, that is the removal of eligible voters who are mistakenly flagged as noncitizens. A rushed process would almost certainly lead to disenfranchisement.”

articles.headline: K/DA Is Getting an Official Louis Vuitton Art Book Ahead of 'Start a Fire' Comeback
keyFacts: Riot Games and Louis Vuitton announced a K/DA travel art book titled Tempo Point featuring illustrations of the virtual group members.
Standard and collector editions of the book will be released on October 16, with prices set at sixty-eight dollars and two hundred forty-five dollars.
The virtual pop group K/DA also teased their first comeback since 2020 with the full project reveal scheduled for October 20.
body: Riot Games has teamed up with fashion house Louis Vuitton on a K/DA Travel Book. The book’s reveal comes just after the League of Legends girl group announced their return from a six-year hiatus.

Tempo Point will collect new illustrations of the virtual girl group, envisioning “24 hours within the individual lives of K/DA members Ahri (vocalist), Akali (rapper), Evelynn (vocalist), and Kai’Sa (vocalist and lead dancer/choreographer).” A Standard edition and Collector’s edition will be released online and in select Louis Vuitton locations and bookstores on Friday, October 16.

The Louis Vuitton Travel Books are a series of premium artbooks, compiling images and illustrations from artists around the world. This particular addition to the collection will be available in two formats: a Standard Edition ($68 USD) and a Collector’s Large-Format Edition ($245 USD). Both editions feature the same artwork in six-color printing, collected in a cloth-bound hardcover book with a silk-screened cover.

Only 400 copies are being printed of the Collector's Edition, which will be available for purchase online on Louis Vuitton’s website , at Louis Vuitton stores, and in select bookstores. The Standard Edition will be available from the same places, and will also be shown off at the upcoming League of Legends Worlds 2026 Fan Fest event scheduled for November 12 to 14 in New York.
Select Louis Vuitton stores will also have limited-edition signed copies that come with an exclusive vinyl record. Only 30 total copies of this edition will be available.
While the Louis Vuitton of it all may seem a bit random, the French fashion house has actually been a consistent collaborator for Riot Games and the virtual girl group.

In 2019, the House served as the official Summoner’s Cup Trophy Trunk provider for the League Worlds Championship. Nicolas Ghesquière, the House’s Artistic Director of Women's Collections, has designed a number of skins for League of Legends, and the House dressed K/DA and guest artist Lexie Liu, who voiced Seraphine, throughout promotions for “MORE.”

K/DA, a virtual pop group which debuted with the single POP/STARS in 2018, just teased their first comeback since 2020. The new project was revealed with an image posted to K/DA social accounts , showing each members’ eyes and the tagline “Start a Fire.” The full project will be revealed on October 20.

articles.headline: YouTuber built 30-frame-per-second grayscale Game Boy, then open sourced it for all e-paper displays
keyFacts: YouTuber Bo Made It created the InkBoy, running Game Boy games at 30 frames per second on an E Ink screen.
Bo built a custom open-source driver to overcome slow E Ink refresh rates and enable four shades of gray.
Bo published the driver on GitHub with a warning that custom waveforms might cause permanent display damage.
body: Sure, running emulated Game Boy games at 30 fps with four shades of gray on an E Ink screen is cool, but you know what's cooler? A custom open source E Ink driver that could theoretically let any display do the same thing. YouTuber Bo Made It published a video last week demonstrating what he calls the InkBoy on a tiny ESP32-S3-powered e-paper board. It looks just about as good as the old-fashioned olive-green screen on the original Game Boy, which isn’t saying much, but it’s an impressive feat to make this work on a cheap stock e-paper screen. For those who haven’t owned an e-reader, E Ink displays are great at what they’re designed for. They can retain what's on the screen without continuously consuming energy by using electrical pulses to move charged pigment particles within individual pixels, enabling them to store the screen state physically. That makes e-paper devices very power efficient, but it comes with a huge trade off: Changing those pixels is a glacially slow process compared with the modern displays we're all accustomed to. The screen that Bo used to make his InkBoy, for example, has a refresh speed of around 300 milliseconds, which is actually on the faster end of e-paper displays - but only really practical for displaying static images. Standard black and white E Ink displays contain two types of pigments: Positively charged black ones, and negatively charged white pigments. Swapping between the two requires a series of brief electrical charges in a particular waveform pattern that gradually move the pixels from the front of the screen to the back, clearing out most of the pigment that shouldn’t be at the surface. The native driver in Bo’s Waveshare 1.54-inch ESP32-S3 e-paper display does just that, and it doesn’t leave a lot of room for displaying motion. In order to get around those limitations, Bo built his own driver for the display that shortened the waveform and enabled per-pixel driving to reduce image ghosting. More impressively, it enabled his ostensibly black and white screen to display four shades of grey, just like an original Game Boy. He was originally using dithering to create greyscale images, but it honestly looked horrible. Luckily Bo noticed something while trying to fix the issue of image ghosting. “I noticed the display was already producing grey - just accidentally,” he said in his video. “The pigment doesn’t instantly jump from black to white, so I wondered if I deliberately stop driving it partway through the transition, can I produce those grey levels on demand?” The answer was yes, and with some additional tweaking he was able to produce those grey levels at 30 frames per second - a vast improvement from the 3.33 frames per second available with the original driver. It’s an impressive accomplishment, but is it a first? Not quite, but it’s still a new way of approaching faster E Ink refresh times. As Bo explains, he got his idea from another YouTuber who built their own E Ink Game Boy, albeit with some entirely custom hardware that allowed them to bypass typical E Ink screen design to create their own faster display. What Bo did was code his own driver for stock hardware, making this an impressive accomplishment in its own right, and one enterprising user could theoretically reproduce on their own if desired. After a month of work, and with the admitted use of some vibe coding for the driver, Bo has published a working version of his driver on GitHub, but with a hefty warning: Not only can forcing custom waveforms and higher refresh rates on E Ink screens cause permanent damage, but long-term panel life wasn’t evaluated as part of his experiment, either. If you’re going to try this, in other words, do so at your own risk, and maybe not on your modded Kindle - buy a cheap E Ink screen to break instead. ®

articles.headline: Renting? These 2 new Apple smart home devices are worth your money (and these 5 are not)
keyFacts: Apple introduced the Apple Home Collection, including new smart home products ranging from $40 sensors to $400 security cameras.
ZDNet reported that specific plug-in devices like the LG Indoor Cam and LG Outdoor Cam work well for renters because they require no permanent installation.
Apple stated that its smart home devices use on-device AI, Private Cloud Compute, and end-to-end encryption to secure user data.
body: Apple recently introduced a handful of new smart home products, with its first smart panel, the HomeView; a new HomePod mini; an Apple TV 4K; and a complete Home Collection with nine smart home devices. Starting at $40 for smart sensors and up to $400 for security cameras, the Apple Home Collection is not exactly budget-friendly, but could it still be right for renters?

As a homeowner with a mix of smart home ecosystems (including Apple Home), I often wonder about the audience companies intend to target with these kinds of devices. I’ve been a renter myself, and I know how creative you have to be with your smart home setup, given landlord and lease restrictions.
More from ZDNET
Good for renters: LG’s Indoor Cam

The LG Indoor Cam is a pan/tilt security camera that looks quite different from comparable options, and has a unique privacy feature. Unlike most indoor cameras that require you to either manually activate privacy mode or set a schedule for it, the Apple Home app triggers it automatically when you come home. While Apple doesn’t specify exactly what triggers this action, it’s likely that it happens based on an iPhone’s location and proximity.

There’s no question that, at $200, the LG Indoor Cam is expensive. There are other indoor cameras with privacy features available, even if they go into privacy mode on a schedule, that are far more affordable and may offer better features, including the $60 Anker Eufy E220, the $140 Anker Eufy S350, and the $99 Aqara Camera Hub G3.
Also: The best iPhone Duo cases in 2026: Expert recommended

The camera itself is attractive and non-descript, resembling a tabletop lamp and breaking away from the usual pan/tilt form factor. It’s great for renters because you don’t have to mount it on a wall (although you can if that’s an option). It also supports AI video search and, with built-in storage, can continue recording during Wi-Fi outages.
Good for renters: LG Outdoor Cam

The LG Outdoor Cam from the Apple Home Collection can work for renters since it’s a plug-in camera; there’s no need to hardwire or replace existing light fixtures, as you have to with the Floodlight Cam.
The Outdoor Cam Plug-in supports 2.5K resolution, color and IR night vision, detection of people, pets, packages, and vehicles, person recognition, and AI-powered video search and descriptions.

This camera can be set up as a bullet camera or tilted downward at an angle. Like Eufy and Reolink cameras, the LG Outdoor Cam can record without Wi-Fi, ensuring you don’t lose important features when the Wi-Fi is out.

At $300, the LG Outdoor Cam follows the same pricing pattern as the rest of the Apple Home Collection. There are more affordable options, however, including the $60 Tapo MagCam and the Blink Outdoor 4, both of which are battery-powered for easier installation in rental properties.
Not so great for renters

Some of the products below aren’t ideal for most renters unless your lease terms are somewhat flexible. If you can get creative with setups, you could still use most of these products in a rental property, but I strongly suggest checking your lease before any installations.

I’ve compiled the remaining Apple Home Collection products with information on what makes them stand out, as well as pricing data, for whom they’re best suited, why they may not be ideal for renters, and some renter-friendly alternatives:
FAQ
Who is Apple’s target audience for the Home Collection?

Apple is appealing to loyalists with its Home Collection. The people who’ve already invested in the Apple ecosystem are the ones Apple wants to buy the Home Collection from. If you already own an iPhone, Apple Watch, HomePod, or an Apple TV device, you can manage new accessories from the same app without downloading a third-party application.
How secure are Apple’s smart home devices?

Apple is ensuring that most AI runs on-device for its new smart home products and that, if this isn’t possible, data goes only through Private Cloud Compute. Apple ensures the company cannot access your footage and emphasizes end-to-end encryption, as well as physical privacy features like those of the LG Indoor Cam.

With HomeKit Secure Video (HKSV), users enjoy intelligent detection, facial recognition, 10 days of recording history with an iCloud+ subscription (though this doesn’t count toward your storage capacity), Apple Home integration with Siri AI descriptions, and local video analysis.
What cameras are compatible with HKSV?

All new LG cameras in the Apple Home Collection are compatible with HKSV, but older cameras also support it. HKSV isn’t new or exclusive to the LG cameras. You can also use it with certain Aqara, Eve, Logitech, Eufy, and Netatmo cameras.

articles.headline: Social Security benefits to get a boost. And, Hasan Piker defends his rhetoric
keyFacts: The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% increase in benefits for next year following a Labor Department inflation report.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced he will resume attacks on Russian oil refineries despite a request from President Trump.
Twitch streamer Hasan Piker stated he is confident he will not hinder Democrats this November after becoming a target for the GOP.
body: Social Security benefits to get a boost. And, Hasan Piker defends his rhetoric
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories

Consumer prices in September were 3.7% higher than they were a year ago, according to a Labor Department report. A spike in energy prices linked to the U.S. war with Iran drove up the cost of living. Excluding energy and food prices, core inflation reached 2.6% in September, up from August. The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% increase in benefits for next year after the release of the inflation report. This annual cost-of-living adjustment is based on prices from July, August and September. Some recipients say the increase is not enough.
- 🎧 Social Security may run out of money to make full payments to retirees as soon as 2032. NPR's Planet Money examines possible solutions.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced he will resume attacks on Russian oil refineries, despite President Trump's request to refrain from doing so. Zelenskyy told the Financial Times that he had ordered commanders to stand down earlier this week, but wouldn't anymore. But Ukraine's ability to conduct these long-range attacks may be limited, as it has seen sudden crippling restrictions to Starshield, the satellite communications system provided by the U.S.

- 🎧 The U.S. is seemingly trying to limit Ukraine's ability to fight Russia, though that has not been announced outright, NPR's Greg Myre tells Up First. Ukraine's defense ministry said today that operations are back to normal. The country relies on the Starshield system for offensive and defensive drones to protect against Russian strikes. Elon Musk, who developed the system for the U.S. government and military, says the U.S. government sets its speed and usage limits.

A man shot and wounded by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in New York last week says he didn't know the men who shot him were ICE agents until after he woke up in the hospital. A new petition filed in Brooklyn federal court says the agents — many of them masked — didn't identify themselves before approaching Oscar Belgal's vehicle with their firearms drawn. The filing contradicts the Trump administration's version of events.

Follow the Newsmakers podcast or subscribe to NPR's YouTube channel to get new episodes as soon as they're available.

California-based Twitch streamer Hasan Piker has emerged as a key target for the GOP ahead of the midterm elections. The president recently labeled him a "terrible liability" and a "communist." In Michigan, political ads attempting to link him to Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayef repeatedly play Piker's most controversial statements, including the infamous "America deserved 9/11." Piker remains confident that he won't hinder Democrats this November. In a conversation with Morning Edition's Leila Fadel, he reflects on his past remarks, the loneliness young men feel and his critique of Tucker Carlson.
Watch or listen to the interview or read the article about their discussion.
Picture show

Australian DJ Lenny Pearce is taking over venues with his toddler rave world tour. Yes, it's is exactly what it sounds like: techno dance parties for families. Most of the dance floor is filled with little ones under the age of five. Around 5 p.m., the speakers blast nursery rhymes like "Bingo" and "The Wheels on the Bus," while the bar offers a refreshing house specialty: apple juice. Pearce kicked off the North American leg of his tour in Baltimore, but has sold-out shows in cities such as New York and Los Angeles and has already captivated audiences in Bahrain, Singapore and India.
